A mirepoix is a fundamental aromatic vegetable base in French cuisine, consisting of diced onions, carrots, and celery cooked slowly in fat without browning to sweeten and build foundational flavor for dishes like stocks, soups, and sauces. Its name derives from the 18th-century French aristocrat, the Duke of Lévis-Mirepoix, though its composition evolved from a meat-inclusive recipe to its modern vegetable form over the 19th century. The traditional ratio is two parts onion to one part carrot and one part celery, though variations exist, including versions with or without meat. Similar foundational vegetable combinations appear globally, such as Italian soffritto, the Cajun holy trinity, and German Suppengrün, highlighting its core culinary principle across cultures.
